name: Lumbar Disc Herniation / PIVD with Radiculopathy
ayurveda: Gridhrasi phenotype correlation where appropriate; structural disc herniation remains a modern anatomical diagnosis
status: Gold chapter draft - source checked, clinician validation pending
synonyms: Lumbar radiculopathy due to disc herniation
definition: Localized displacement of lumbar disc material beyond the normal margins of the intervertebral disc space that becomes clinically relevant when it produces concordant nerve-root irritation or compression, causing radicular pain and/or neurological deficit. Imaging alone does not establish symptomatic disc herniation; symptoms, examination and the level/side of neural compression must correlate.
classification: Disc morphology: bulge (not a focal herniation), protrusion, extrusion and sequestration/migration.
Location: central, paracentral/subarticular, foraminal or extraforaminal/far-lateral.
Clinical phenotype: radicular pain without objective deficit; sensory-predominant radiculopathy; motor deficit; cauda equina syndrome; recurrent or postoperative herniation.
Most clinically important symptomatic levels are L4-L5 and L5-S1.
pathophysiology: Radicular symptoms arise from a combination of mechanical compression and inflammatory/chemical irritation of the affected nerve root.
A paracentral L4-L5 herniation commonly affects the traversing L5 root; a paracentral L5-S1 herniation commonly affects S1.
Far-lateral/foraminal herniations more often affect the exiting root at that level, for example L4 at L4-L5.
Disc fragments can regress or resorb over time; spontaneous reduction is particularly reported with extruded/sequestered morphology.
presentation: Leg-dominant pain radiating from buttock into thigh/leg/foot in a root-related pattern, often with associated low back pain.
Paresthesia, numbness or dysesthesia in a dermatomal tendency.
Myotomal weakness may occur, including dorsiflexion weakness/foot drop or plantar-flexion weakness.
Coughing, sneezing, straining, sitting or spinal flexion may aggravate symptoms in some patients.
Straight Leg Raise may reproduce radicular symptoms in lower-lumbar root involvement; crossed SLR is less sensitive but more specific when positive.
Symptoms and neurological findings may fluctuate; severity of pain does not always equal severity of motor deficit.
redFlags: CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME: new urinary retention or overflow incontinence, new fecal dysfunction, saddle/perineal sensory loss, bilateral severe sciatica, or rapidly progressive bilateral neurological deficit.
Rapidly progressive or severe motor deficit, including evolving foot drop.
Major trauma, fracture risk or spinal instability.
Fever, bacteremia risk, immunosuppression, IV drug use or concern for spinal infection/epidural abscess.
Known malignancy, unexplained weight loss or destructive/systemic features suggesting cancer.
Symptoms suggesting a vascular, abdominal, pelvic or other non-spinal emergency.
Pain plus upper-motor-neuron signs or neurological findings that do not fit a single lumbar root should trigger diagnostic reconsideration.
history: Exact pain and numbness map: back, buttock, thigh, calf, dorsum/sole of foot and individual toes.
Onset, lifting/trauma event, duration, progression, recurrence and previous episodes.
Aggravating/relieving factors: sitting, walking, flexion, cough/sneeze/strain and lying positions.
Motor symptoms: knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion, great-toe extension, plantar flexion, repeated heel/toe walking and foot slap.
Mandatory cauda equina screen when clinically indicated: bladder, bowel, saddle sensation, sexual function and bilateral symptoms.
Past cancer, infection risk, steroid exposure, osteoporosis, anticoagulation, inflammatory disease and prior lumbar surgery.
Previous MRI, injections, medications, physiotherapy and response.
Functional impact: walking, sleep, work, driving, sitting tolerance and ADL.
Recovery modifiers: fear-avoidance, work conflict, mood/sleep disturbance and patient expectations.
exam: Gait, heel walking, toe walking and observation for foot drop or antalgic posture.
Motor testing: L2 hip flexion, L3 knee extension, L4 ankle dorsiflexion contribution, L5 great-toe extension/ankle dorsiflexion, S1 plantar flexion/eversion; document MRC grade when weak.
Sensory testing in dermatomal distributions with side-to-side comparison.
Reflexes: patellar (predominantly L3-L4) and Achilles (predominantly S1).
Supine Straight Leg Raise / Lasègue for L4-S1 radicular irritation; crossed SLR when relevant.
Femoral nerve stretch test for upper-lumbar L2-L4 radicular patterns.
Slump test can supplement neural-tension assessment but should be interpreted in the total clinical picture.
Hip examination and peripheral nerve examination when competing diagnoses are plausible.
Check pulses/vascular status when vascular claudication or limb ischemia is a concern.

rootMap.typicalDisc: L2-L3 or L3-L4 depending on location

rootMap.motor: knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion contribution
rootMap.typicalDisc: usually L3-L4 traversing root; L4-L5 far-lateral/exiting root

rootMap.sensory: lateral leg, dorsum of foot, great-toe tendency
rootMap.motor: great-toe extension, ankle dorsiflexion, hip abduction

differentials: Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
Facet-mediated or non-specific axial low back pain
Hip osteoarthritis, labral pathology or greater-trochanteric pain syndrome
Common peroneal neuropathy or other peripheral nerve entrapment
Spinal infection, malignancy, fracture or inflammatory disease
investigations: MRI lumbar spine without contrast is the preferred non-invasive test to confirm a suspected disc herniation when imaging is clinically indicated.

In patients without significant neurological deficit, WFNS recommends radiological assessment when persistent symptoms remain after roughly 6-12 weeks; earlier imaging is appropriate with motor deficit or red flags.
Do not order routine MRI for every acute episode of sciatica when symptoms are improving and no red flags are present; imaging should answer a management-changing question.
MRI with contrast is reserved for selected postoperative, infection, tumor or inflammatory questions.
CT or CT myelography can be used when MRI is contraindicated or for specific bony/specialist questions.
Electrodiagnostic testing is useful when the clinical level is uncertain, symptoms are atypical, peripheral neuropathy/plexopathy is a competing diagnosis, or imaging and examination do not agree.
Targeted laboratory tests are used only when infection, inflammatory disease or malignancy is suspected.
imagingCorrelation: Document level, side and location: central, paracentral/subarticular, foraminal or far-lateral.
Describe morphology: protrusion, extrusion, sequestration/migration; avoid calling every broad bulge a herniation.
Identify which root is compressed: traversing versus exiting root.
Report lateral recess, foraminal and central canal compromise separately.
MRI severity must be interpreted with the neurological pattern; a large asymptomatic herniation can exist, while a smaller strategically placed foraminal fragment can be highly symptomatic.
Note additional findings relevant to treatment planning: disc height loss, Modic change, facet arthropathy, spondylolisthesis, congenital canal narrowing or prior surgery.
management: When there is no cauda equina syndrome or major/progressive motor deficit, initial management is usually nonoperative because many patients improve and disc material may regress over time.
Maintain tolerable activity; avoid prolonged bed rest. Short relative rest may be reasonable during severe acute pain, followed by progressive activity.
Use individualized rehabilitation: directional-preference exercises where appropriate, trunk/hip conditioning, neural mobility when tolerated, walking and graded return to work/activity.
Medication decisions require patient-specific gastrointestinal, renal, cardiovascular, hepatic, pregnancy and interaction risk assessment; the chapter should not auto-generate drug prescriptions.

NICE advises against gabapentinoids/other antiepileptics, oral corticosteroids and benzodiazepines for sciatica because overall benefit is lacking and harms exist; chronic opioids are not recommended.

Epidural local anaesthetic plus steroid can be considered for acute severe sciatica in a specialist pathway; benefit is generally symptom-focused and does not replace emergency surgery when major neurological compromise is present.
Urgent surgical/spine assessment is required for cauda equina syndrome and progressive or severe motor deficit.
Surgical decompression/discectomy is appropriate to consider when non-surgical treatment has not improved pain/function and MRI findings are concordant with the sciatic symptoms.

WFNS recommends individualized surgery for failed conservative care, severe motor deficit, progressive neurological impairment or cauda equina syndrome; earlier surgery is favored when major motor deficit is present.
Routine fusion is not indicated after primary discectomy for an isolated herniated disc without instability or another specific fusion indication.
rehab: Acute high-irritability phase: education, positions of comfort, short frequent walks, pain-limited mobility and avoidance of repeated provocative loading.
Recovery phase: restore lumbar/hip mobility as needed, progressive trunk and hip strength, gait normalization and graded neural mobility if tolerated.
Functional phase: progressive sitting, driving, lifting/hinge practice, work simulation and aerobic conditioning.
Motor deficit requires serial objective reassessment rather than pain-only follow-up.
After discectomy, rehabilitation should follow the surgeon's restrictions and then progress toward walking, trunk/hip conditioning and task-specific loading.
Reassess urgently for new saddle sensory change, bladder/bowel dysfunction, rapidly worsening weakness or bilateral neurological symptoms.
outcomes: Motor MRC grade by affected root

ayurvedaFramework.vyadhi: Gridhrasi may correlate with a radicular pain phenotype, especially when buttock-to-leg radiation and functional limitation are present, but lumbar disc herniation itself is a modern structural diagnosis and should remain explicitly documented.
ayurvedaFramework.principle: Use parallel documentation: modern localization and red-flag assessment first, followed by Ayurvedic Nidana-Samprapti assessment. Do not allow a Gridhrasi label to obscure cauda equina syndrome, severe motor deficit, tumor, infection or fracture.
assessment: Vataja versus Vata-Kaphaja clinical phenotype where defensible
Relevant Vata subtypes and Avarana considerations
Functional impact and neurological deficit documented separately from Ayurvedic descriptors
ayurvedaFramework.clinicalFeatures: Record the exact radicular distribution, sensory changes, motor power, reflexes and MRI localization before mapping the Ayurvedic phenotype.
ayurvedaFramework.treatmentSafety: Nidana Parivarjana, Shamana, Basti and external/Panchakarma procedures require individualized assessment. Forceful spinal manipulation or delay of referral is unsafe when cauda equina syndrome, progressive motor weakness, fracture, infection, malignancy or major neurological compromise is suspected.

patientHandout: A lumbar disc herniation means some disc material has moved beyond its normal boundary. It matters clinically when it irritates or compresses a nerve root and matches your symptoms and examination.

Many patients improve without surgery, and herniated disc material can shrink over time. Staying gently active and following a graded rehabilitation program is usually preferred to prolonged bed rest.
MRI is most useful when symptoms persist, neurological weakness is present, red flags exist, or a procedure/surgery is being considered.
Seek urgent care for new difficulty passing urine, loss of bladder/bowel control, numbness around the saddle/genital area, rapidly worsening leg weakness or severe bilateral neurological symptoms.
Surgery may be considered when disabling leg pain or neurological deficit does not improve with appropriate non-surgical care and the MRI finding matches the affected nerve root.
An MRI report should never be interpreted by size alone; the level, side, location and clinical neurological findings must agree.
